Alaska.Ai — Received Wisdom Draft

2026-06-02 · branch claude/linkedin-contrarian-2026-06-02

Copy this for LinkedIn

Alaska’s court system built an AI chatbot to do the job of a human self-help facilitator. The bot then pointed a user to alumni of an Alaska law school that does not exist.

The chatbot is named AVA, and its design goal was stated plainly. Stacey Marz, Administrative Director of the Alaska Court System, told NBC News in January that the aim was “to basically try to replicate the services with the chatbot that we would provide with a human facilitator.” Replicate, not assist. That word is doing a lot of work, and it is the word worth examining.

The ambition is sound. Alaska runs roughly 7,000 self-represented litigants through its courts each year, across a state larger than Texas, with no law school and thin legal aid. For most rural Alaskans, the realistic alternative to a facilitator isn’t a different facilitator. It’s no help at all. A reliable chatbot answering routine procedural questions at 2am, every day, would genuinely extend access. Marz and her team aimed at the right north star.

Where it breaks is reliability, and the court has said so itself. Beyond the invented law school, Marz acknowledged in the same article that “we’re not confident that the bots can work in that fashion, because of the issues with some inaccuracies and some incompleteness.” The validated test-question set was cut from 91 down to 16. A three-month project ran more than 18 months past target. Replication of a facilitator demands near-perfect accuracy on consequential legal questions. A general-purpose model can’t guarantee that, and AVA confirmed it on the exact high-stakes question a human handles well.

There’s a second primary source pointing the same direction. A peer-reviewed Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence paper from April 2025, authored across Stanford, ANTHC, UAF, Southcentral Foundation, and Maniilaq, found that high-consequence AI deployment in Alaska needs community-engaged methodology and multi-year data integration. The authors note only 0.2 percent of more than 1,000 AI healthcare papers even mention community involvement. The field is not ready to replicate human judgment in Alaska-specific settings.

The more accurate frame isn’t “AI can’t help courts.” It’s that the design target should be augmentation on bounded, high-confidence procedural queries, not replication of open-ended judgment. The failure modes land hardest on the most legally vulnerable Alaskans. Anyone underwriting an Alaska justice, health, or social-services AI deployment on a replacement assumption should re-price the reliability gap AVA exposed before the next launch, not after. That list includes court procurement officers, govtech vendors, and federal grant writers.

Where should the line sit between a procedural question an Alaska court bot can safely answer and one that still demands a human?

#AlaskaAI #AIPolicy #RuralHealth #ProcurementReform #HealthcareAI

Sources

  • NBC News (syndicated via AOL) — 2026-01-03 — Claim asserter and primary counter-evidence — Stacey Marz on the AVA chatbot built to replicate a human facilitator; same article documents the hallucinated non-existent Alaska law school, her walk-back, the 91 to 16 test-question cut, and the 18-plus-month overrun on a 3-month project.
  • Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence / PubMed Central — 2025-04-01 — Counter-evidence — Rice et al. (Stanford, ANTHC, UAF, Southcentral Foundation, Maniilaq) on high-consequence AI deployment in Alaska needing community-engaged methodology; only 0.2 percent of 1,000-plus AI healthcare papers even mention community involvement.

Editor's report card

CriterionScoreWeightNotes
Hook strength100.13First two lines name the load-bearing claim (AI replicating human facilitator) and immediately signal the correction (law school that does not exist) with zero snark. Well under the 210-char LinkedIn cutoff and stands alone as a complete hook.
Claim load-bearing + AK stakes80.2Claim is genuinely load-bearing (active procurement, late-January 2026 launch, federal grant positioning). Correction names concrete audience (court procurement officers, govtech vendors, federal grant writers) and sector (access-to-justice AI). Drops one point because no dollar amount or contract number is cited; the consequence is real but the financial magnitude is unquantified.
Steelman fairness100.12Paragraph 3 is a generous, structurally accurate steelman: 7,000 litigants, state-larger-than-Texas geography, no law school, thin legal aid, and explicitly says the ambition is sound and aimed at the right north star before any rebuttal. A believer in the claim would feel fairly represented. Matches dossier steelman text.
Counter-evidence quality100.1Two rebuttal pillars: (1) Marz's own walk-back quote, invented law school hallucination, 91-to-16 test set cut, 18-month project overrun, all primary source (NBC News, in dossier). (2) Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence April 2025 peer-reviewed paper, multi-institution (Stanford, ANTHC, UAF, Southcentral Foundation, Maniilaq), PMC-indexed, primary. Both entries present in claim_dossier.json counter_evidence.
Factual density90.1Named specifics appear in nearly every sentence: Stacey Marz, NBC News, AVA, 7,000 litigants, state larger than Texas, no law school, 91 to 16, three-month project, 18 months past target, April 2025, Stanford/ANTHC/UAF/Southcentral Foundation/Maniilaq, 0.2 percent, more than 1,000 papers. One connective sentence in paragraph 4 is purely analytical with no named fact, preventing a 10.
Source quality100.13Claim attribution traces to a primary source (Marz directly quoted in NBC News). Both counter-evidence entries are primary: the same NBC News article and a peer-reviewed Frontiers in AI paper on PMC. All sourcing traces to claim_dossier.json.
Voice match90.12Analytical and position-taking throughout. Business-literate without influencer cadence. Corrective without contempt. One minor formulaic phrase is slightly newsletter-template but does not break character.
Readability (LinkedIn)90.05Paragraphs are 2 to 4 sentences. Word count within 350 to 475 range. Total character count well under 3,000. No wall-of-text. Scans cleanly on mobile and desktop.
Engagement question100.03Closing question is real and debatable and tied directly to the corrected frame of augmentation versus replication. No rhetorical softener, no CTA.
Business actionability100.02Final paragraph names exactly who should act and what to do: court procurement officers, govtech vendors, and federal grant writers should re-price the reliability gap before the next launch.

Weighted total: 9.33 / 10 · Threshold: 8.0 · Ship: yes
